findings.title: f32→f64 contract upcast is asserted but does not exist; wire serializer would emit corrupted output
findings.description: The "f32/f64 contract" paragraph states: "`export_positions()` and `export_velocities()` return f64 arrays (Quadrants upcasts on download). The `TickResult` therefore carries f64, preserving the downstream contract." Both premises are contradicted by the components the design builds on. The existing `GpuAgentState.export_positions()`/`export_velocities()` explicitly return f32 arrays (`NDArray[np.float32]`, with an explicit `astype(np.float32)`), and `TickResult.from_quadrants_fields()` is documented to wrap pre-downloaded arrays "without allocation or dtype conversion" — "we pass through whatever the caller gave us so f32 input arrays remain f32." No upcast happens at download or at TickResult construction. The downstream consumer named in A3 (`client_manager.broadcast` → `protocol.serialize_state_update`) writes `result.positions.tobytes()` into a wire layout documented as `positions_f64 | velocities_f64`; the sim logger serializes through the same function. If f32 arrays flow in as designed, the wire and log payloads are silently corrupted (4-byte floats where 8-byte doubles are expected), and A3 ("same dtype contract as the CPU path… zero changes") fails. The design must state where the f32→f64 conversion happens (e.g., in `GpuSimulationDriver.step()` before constructing the `TickResult`, or in a modified export), and note that the Files-Changed table lists only `setup_from_server()` and `upload_positions()` as `agent_state.py` additions — no export change.

findings.title: GPU path never writes results back to `EntityManager.state`; snapshots and spawn/despawn sync operate on permanently stale CPU state
findings.description:
On the CPU path, `tick()` mutates the `AgentState` owned by `EntityManager` in place (the `TickResult` is a view over it — `from_numpy_state`), so `em.state` is live every tick. The design's GPU data flow (§Data Flow, §SimulationManager Changes) exports fresh copies into the `TickResult` and has **no** GPU→CPU write-back; the only state transfer toward the driver is `sync_from_entity_manager()` (CPU→GPU). Consequences the design does not address:
1. The client snapshot path (`make_snapshot_builder`, which builds `TickResult.from_numpy_state(em.state, em.count)` on every new-client connect) serves **spawn-time** positions forever on the GPU path — the "at worst one tick stale" bound that path documents becomes unbounded staleness. This directly contradicts A3's "Downstream code (client_manager.broadcast, sim logger) requires zero changes."
2. `sync_from_entity_manager()` "re-uploads CPU state after spawn/despawn" wholesale — but on the GPU path that CPU state is stale, so any spawn/despawn mid-run would teleport all surviving agents back to their last-CPU-state positions and destroy the GPU tick's evolution. This corrupts the very spawn/despawn sync the slice plan assigns to this slice.
3. `EntityManager.get_position()` and any other runtime reader of `em.state` see stale data.
The design needs a per-tick write-back of the downloaded arrays into `em.state` (cheap — the arrays are already host-side), or an explicit redefinition of what `EntityManager` owns on the GPU path plus corresponding changes to the snapshot builder.

findings.title: `GpuAgentState.setup_from_server()` signature inverts the dependency direction (engine package → server package)
findings.description: The design moves `GpuAgentState` to `src/migratory/gpu/agent_state.py` — inside the `migratory` engine package — and gives it `setup_from_server(self, entity_manager: EntityManager, ..., world_bounds: WorldBoundsConfig, ...)`. `EntityManager` lives in `migratory_server.entities` and `WorldBoundsConfig` in `migratory_server.config`. Today the `migratory` package has zero imports of `migratory_server` (only docstring mentions); this signature would create the first engine→server dependency and a package import cycle (`migratory_server.simulation` → `migratory.gpu.agent_state` → `migratory_server.entities`/`config`), violating the layering the move to `src/migratory/gpu/` is supposed to establish. The clean fix: `setup_from_server` (or a renamed `setup_from_state`) takes the engine-type `AgentState` (which `EntityManager.state` already returns, and which carries the `leadership` array the Open Notes reference) plus primitive width/height/dt/subdivision_factor; the driver — which lives in `migratory_server` and may import both sides — does the extraction from `EntityManager`/`WorldBoundsConfig`. Note the engine package already has a `WorldBounds` type (`migratory.environment`) that `simulation.py` already knows how to build from `WorldBoundsConfig`.

findings.title: No-GPU fallback contract is self-contradictory: `_select_arch()` cannot deliver A7, and Open Notes make the same scenario fatal
findings.description: Scope and A7 promise: "falls back to CPU with a logged warning if neither is detected… The server does not crash." But the specified `_select_arch()` checks only `platform.system()` — it returns `qd.cuda` unconditionally on **any** Linux host, with no GPU-capability probe, so a Linux box without CUDA (exactly A7's scenario, and the most common no-GPU host) reaches `qd.init(arch=qd.cuda)`. Open Notes then state the opposite behavior for that exact case: "If `qd.init()` raises (e.g. CUDA driver absent…) the server exits at startup." Both cannot hold; as written, A7 passes only on platforms that are neither Darwin nor Linux. The warning text ("No supported GPU detected for platform") also claims a detection the code does not perform. Additionally, if the intended fix is "catch the failed `qd.init` and retry with `qd.cpu`," that requires a second `qd.init()` in the same process — which the same Open Notes call undefined behavior. The design must pick one contract (probe capability before `qd.init`, or accept fatal exit and restate A7/Scope accordingly) and specify the detection mechanism.

findings.title: Spawn/despawn sync under-specified: count-proxy misses net-zero transitions; buffer growth policy unstated
findings.description: The dirty-detection helper `count_changed_since_last_tick()` treats count identity as state identity. The `EntityManager` API allows `spawn_entity`/`spawn_population` and `remove_entity` between ticks; one spawn plus one remove in the same inter-tick window leaves the count unchanged while the state arrays change (and `remove_entity` index-shifts all downstream agents), so the re-upload is silently skipped and GPU state diverges from CPU state. The plan entry requires "re-upload **changed agent state**," not "changed count" — a dirty flag set by the `EntityManager` mutators (spawn/remove) is the robust mechanism and costs no per-tick work. Separately, `GpuAgentState` fields are allocated at `setup()` for the initial `n`; the design never says whether `sync_from_entity_manager()` reallocates GPU fields when the population grows (or caps at `EntityManager._capacity` and tracks a live count), so the "spawn increases N" case has no stated handling — a new host↔device path with an unenumerated failure mode.

findings.title: Test plan contradicts the design's own `qd.init()` process-isolation constraint
findings.description: Open Notes state: "the second `qd.init()` in the same process is undefined behavior. Tests that exercise `GpuSimulationDriver.setup()` must either use `finalize()` + process isolation or be marked to run in a subprocess." Yet unit tests 5–8 each construct a driver and call `setup()` (which calls `qd.init`) inside the same `tests/server/test_gpu_driver.py` module, with no statement that they run in separate subprocesses; test 8 ("finalize is idempotent") even chains off test 5's setup. The section is also internally inconsistent about where tests execute: "All tests are CPU-only" vs. "Where Quadrants is available on Metal (CI Mac), tests run on Metal; on CUDA Linux they run on CUDA." Specify the isolation mechanism per test (e.g., a subprocess fixture for every setup-exercising test) and reconcile the CPU-only statement.

findings.title: Deferred `_positions_dirty` sync-back is a heavier mechanism than the requirement needs
findings.description: The sync-back design adds `notify_positions_modified()` storing a retained array reference, an internal `_positions_dirty` flag, and an upload deferred to the start of the next `step()`. The stated requirement is only that the GPU state reflects post-bounds positions before the next kernel use; calling `state.upload_positions(...)` **immediately** inside `notify_positions_modified()` meets it with no cross-tick retained state, no flag, no ordering constraint inside `step()`, and a smaller test surface (and it can piggyback on any write-back added per the `EntityManager.state` finding). The design gives no reason the upload must be deferred (e.g., further in-place mutation by `environment.post_tick()`, which the CPU path's lifecycle says writes agent-originated writes *to the environment*, not to agents). Cut the deferred mechanism unless a concrete consumer of the deferral is named.

findings.title: Files-Changed table names a non-existent module
findings.description: The table lists `src/migratory_server/entity_manager.py` for the `count_changed_since_last_tick()` helper, but `EntityManager` lives in `src/migratory_server/entities.py`; there is no `entity_manager.py` in the tree. Rename the row so implementers edit the right module.

findings.title: Tier 2 gate does not pin the workload regime the milestone is defined against
findings.description: `tests/load/test_gpu_server_tps.py` asserts "TPS ≥ 60" at "50k agents" but specifies no world size/density, profile mix, or `subdivision_factor`, while the plan's Tier 2 target (and slices 148–149's exit criteria) is "≥60 TPS at N=50k **mid-flock-density**," and the Open Notes recommend S=3 for N≥10k two-flock density. The NFR is restated with its numeric target (good), but without a pinned workload the gate evidence is not comparable to the 148/149 measurements that justify it — state the workload config the gate runs (or reference the slice-141 workload id).
